Research can be quantitative (statistics, surveys, questionnaires) or qualitative (expressions, emotions, body language). Under GDPR we protect not only individual items of personal data but also combinations that could identify a person.

Research clients need to know who answered so they can make sense of the results. A finding like "people prefer the new design" is far more useful when researchers can see that younger people preferred it while older people didn't, or that parents and non-parents answered differently. That's why surveys ask about demographics, household, work and lifestyle.

Research findings feed into decisions on very different timelines. An advert might be adjusted within weeks of testing. A packaging change might take months. A new product or software feature could take a year or more to reach the market. You'll rarely know which specific change your answer influenced, but collectively, the opinions of research participants shape a surprising amount of what appears in shops, apps and services.

Research works by combining many answers. Each response shifts the overall picture slightly – and some findings hinge on small differences between groups. If careless or fraudulent answers creep in, the picture becomes distorted. That's why honest, attentive answers are so valuable, and why research companies invest in quality controls and verification.

Researchers analyse the data: percentages, comparisons between groups, statistical tests and themes from open-ended answers. Your words in open-ended questions often appear (anonymously) as quotes that bring numbers to life.

Researchers know that people in different cultures sometimes answer rating questions differently – some tend towards the middle of a scale, others towards the extremes. Good research design accounts for this when comparing countries. For you as a participant, the advice is simple: answer naturally and honestly. You don't need to adjust your answers to match what you think people elsewhere would say. Genuine responses from your own perspective are exactly what international studies need.
Researchers prefer honest uncertainty to guesses.

You'll sometimes see platforms describe themselves as "GDPR compliant" or offering "GDPR surveys". In practice, compliance means a company has a lawful basis for processing your data (usually your consent for research), explains its purposes clearly, keeps data only as long as needed, protects it with appropriate security and lets you exercise your rights. It also means research partners handling data on the company's behalf are bound by the same obligations.
